name: Cosmic pessimism: Will as evil
plain_explanation: Unlike thinkers who might identify the one universal Will with God and urge conformity to it (as Spinoza does), Schopenhauer holds the Will itself is wicked -- the very source of all suffering -- since willing has no fixed end that, once achieved, would bring lasting contentment; unfulfilled desire causes pain, and even satisfied desire brings only fleeting satiety before the cycle begins again.
precise_definition: Schopenhauer's ethical verdict on the metaphysical Will: it is the source of all suffering, since it is essentially endless striving without any final satisfaction, such that 'there is no such thing as happiness, for an unfulfilled wish causes pain, and attainment brings only satiety'; suffering is thus not accidental but essential to all life and is increased, not decreased, by increased knowledge.
why_it_mattered: This is what makes Schopenhauer, unusually among voluntarist philosophers, a pessimist -- a combination Russell calls 'only possible for a pessimist,' since most later thinkers who prioritized will (e.g. Nietzsche) found in it grounds for optimism instead.
historical_origin: The World as Will and Idea.
examples: The soap-bubble image: 'we blow out a soap-bubble as long and as large as possible, although we know perfectly well that it will burst'
Shame associated with the sexual act, since procreation creates new occasions for suffering and death
objections: Russell: 'From a scientific point of view, optimism and pessimism are alike objectionable: optimism assumes... that the universe exists to please us, and pessimism that it exists to displease us. Scientifically, there is no evidence that it is concerned with us either one way or the other.'
competing_positions: The predominant optimistic temperament Russell says has been 'much commoner among Western philosophers'
Later voluntarists (Nietzsche, Bergson) who affirm will without Schopenhauer's pessimism
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell credits Schopenhauer's pessimism with a historically useful function: making it possible 'for men to take to philosophy without having to persuade themselves that all evil can be explained away.'
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Leads directly to Schopenhauer's preference for Buddhism and Hinduism over Christianity.
